rationale: A wins because it separates story from wishful thinking and makes the proof burden explicit. Its angle, "The $550 claim: what a flight-deal subscription actually saves, and how it's counted," is exactly the kind of uncomfortable service story a reporter can defend. B has good bones, but it keeps "From Scott's Cheap Flights to Going to AI trip planner: a deal-alert brand's long reinvention," which turns one supplied rebrand fact into a whole founder-profile arc. That is how a decent angle set walks itself into a fact-check ditch.
gaps_in_A: "Going's AI trip planner turns a $200 mistake fare into a booked week" invents a $200 fare and implies an actual booked trip. The update gives no fare amount and says booking does not happen in-app.
"the free tier finds the fare" is plausible but not explicitly in the supplied facts. Don't build the paywall thesis on an unstated tier behavior without confirming it.
"Story type: funding-mechanics" is the wrong label for a subscription-conversion angle. There is no funding story here.
"the prevailing assumption is that AI travel tools are racing to own booking" is outside the update. It may be true, but this judging brief did not give it to you.
gaps_in_B: "From Scott's Cheap Flights to Going to AI trip planner: a deal-alert brand's long reinvention" is overbuilt. The update says formerly Scott's Cheap Flights; it does not supply a founder story, newsletter history, reinvention timeline, or company-evolution arc.
"the prevailing model in AI travel tools is intent-first" is an unsupported market claim. Nice thesis, thin sourcing.
"tech business reporter covering SaaS subscription models" is sloppy beat-matching. Going is a consumer travel subscription, not SaaS just because there is a paywall.
"flight-deal newsletter" and "deal-detection engine" are not in the update. Small invented details are still invented details.
